title: Bad Trips Guide, Round 43
intro: Round 43 (2026-11-19). Your round-42 answer is in. This turn took the Medium and Low windows of the first batch, the way your round-41 versions showed: each paragraph checked by itself as the guide has it first, then from that near miss a word or two a reader could take two ways, checked after each change ([every check](https://github.com/u-dont-existDOTcom/joel-articles/blob/claude/bad-trips-20261105/articles/bad-trips/humanize/h57-20261119/RESULTS.md)).

Ten paragraphs read Human High by themselves as they already stood, and seven more do now and are in: DMSO's side effects, niacin's side effects and its other forms, Get One Human Anchor's backup line, the ordinary-world list, Shadow Work's opening and the Appendix's list. Two of mine didn't move in three tries each, so they are this round's two cards: how you'd say them teaches me the ones like them.

suggestions.title: 1. DMSO beside aged ozonated-charcoal water: which to give, or both
suggestions.reading: By itself, as the guide has it: [Human Written, two windows Medium](https://www.pangram.com/history/2da90d18-b6ed-485d-8e6e-b25258a0cda0), "Sometimes DMSO works better; sometimes the water does." (9 words) and the last sentence (19 words); the rest High.
suggestions.tested:
Both semicolon pairs joined with "and", "in my experience" said once: [the same two Medium windows](https://www.pangram.com/history/137ef380-fff3-4675-9d16-e7a9e92f3351).

"Sometimes DMSO calms a trip better, and sometimes the charcoal water does." (what each does better, and which water): [worse, Medium over the first four sentences and Low on the last](https://www.pangram.com/history/7549911f-5de2-4da7-81e2-777652365122), though the last sentence was word for word the guide's.
suggestions.sense: Three fresh readers each time. Read alone, "It" points at nothing (in the guide it is DMSO, named in your paragraph before); "Sometimes ... sometimes" gives no way to choose; "taking both or mixing them" could mean one after the other or in one drink; and "perfect safety profile" read to one reader like a drug label, reassuring more than one person's experience can.
suggestions.why: It is your experience, in your voice, and three small changes didn't move its windows (the third made them worse). How you would say which to give, and that both is fine, teaches me the other first-person remedy paragraphs still Medium.
suggestions.advice_note: Edit it: the paragraph in your words. Your version goes in whole.

suggestions.title: 2. Dealing With Shadow Thoughts: why the opposite thought shows up
suggestions.reading: With the identity line before it, by itself: [Human, the last sentence Medium](https://www.pangram.com/history/7d46b28c-82de-4c65-a74d-af218111b4e4) ("In the subconscious world of concepts, however, two sides are often considered together.", 13 words); the rest High.
suggestions.tested:
"In the subconscious world of concepts, however, the mind often keeps both together." (who considers them, and which two): [Medium again](https://www.pangram.com/history/a4b0fea1-f9bb-472b-a32c-2a383f29e503).

"In the subconscious world of concepts, though, each idea often comes paired with its opposite." (what happens to a concept): [Medium again](https://www.pangram.com/history/8479bdd0-0087-4b23-ae89-e3d0ea85def7).
suggestions.sense: Fresh readers: "the subconscious world of concepts" can be read several ways, and "the two sides" could be love and hate or the Hermetic opposites. One reader, in a dark moment, heard "a hated baby does not feel love" as being about their own past before it turned out to be an example, and another found the first three sentences (unweaving the identity illusion, your pamphlet, the Hermetic claim) give such a reader nothing to hold; I changed none of those, since they are your teaching and read High.
suggestions.why: The last sentence is the one that says why opposite thoughts come, and it stays Medium in every wording I tried. How you would say it teaches me the other lines in the shadow part that explain the mind.
suggestions.advice_note: Edit it: the last sentence, or the paragraph, in your words. If you'd also change the sentences before it, they are yours to.
